title: Dominoes & Dice Games
strapline: Spots you can read at a glance, and games where taking turns is half the maths.
intent: Children learn to subitise — to see two, three or four spots at a glance without counting each one.
Children match, compare and combine amounts through the natural rules of domino and dice games.
Children rehearse turn-taking, fairness and coping with winning and losing in a warm, low-stakes way.
Children begin to add by combining two dice or two ends of a domino and finding the total.
Children build the counting-and-comparing language that games make necessary — more, fewer, the same, altogether.
implementation: Offer chunky dominoes and large-dot dice, plus giant floor versions for whole-body play.
Play alongside, thinking aloud: 'I can see four without counting — how did you know it was three?'
Start with matching games (find a domino with the same number of spots) before scoring games.
Encourage subitising by flashing a dice briefly: 'quick — how many?' then checking together.
Introduce simple totalling — roll two dice, count on to find how many altogether — when children are ready.
Model turn-taking and good sportsmanship gently: 'your go next', 'well rolled', 'unlucky, try again'.
Keep a set outdoors and a set at snack so games happen in odd pockets of the day, not just at 'maths time'.
key_questions: How many spots — can you tell without counting?
Can you find a domino that matches this one?
How many altogether on both dice?
Who rolled more this time — how do you know?

impact.text: Children recognise small amounts of spots at a glance.
Children match and compare quantities on dominoes and dice.
Children combine two amounts and find the total by counting on.
Children take turns, follow rules and manage winning and losing.
Children use comparing language — more, fewer, the same, altogether.
Children stay engaged with a game to the end and want to play again.

enhancements: Giant floor dominoes and foam dice for a whole-body version.
Home-made dominoes using children's own photos or nature marks instead of spots.
A 'roll and cover' board game where dice decide which square to fill.
Number-track games where a dice roll moves a counter along.
A pot of two dice for a 'total challenge' — race to reach ten.
Blank dice to draw their own spots or symbols and invent new rules.

playing_exploring: Children choose and adapt games, inventing their own rules.
The quick 'how many?' flash makes subitising a game they love.
active_learning: Children stick with a game across many turns, wanting to finish.
They cope with an unlucky roll and try again.
creating_thinking: Children work out totals and compare amounts to decide who's ahead.
They invent new rules and predict who might win.
